nm:statphys-levy-local-time-identity.why: Source claim: Rogers states Theorem 2 (Lévy) on p. 311, and Mörters and Peres prove it as Theorem 7.38 on p. 212. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the identity gives the law of the local time at 0 and is a key step to excursion theory, so res is 3. The proof is short when Tanaka's formula and Lévy's characterization are available, so pro is 3.

review.conditions: B starts at 0, and L is the Tanaka local time at 0 with the occupation-density normalization. The equality in law is for the processes on C([0, ∞), ℝ²), so it is stronger than a statement at a fixed time. The a.s. limit with ≤ ε is true because the occupation measure has a continuous density.
review.prerequisites: Tanaka's formula gives |B| = W + L. Lévy's characterization identifies W as a Brownian motion from ⟨W⟩_t = t. Tonelli shows that the zero set has Lebesgue measure 0. The Tanaka record also gives that L is nondecreasing and grows only on the zero set, so step s3 has 2 sources. wd:Q7820874 has an open identity conflict, but the use is the product-measure theorem.
review.alignment: I read p. 311 of the local copy of Rogers. Theorem 2 states (S, S − B) =𝒟 (L, |B|) with L = L(t, 0), the Trotter density. The record lists the same pairs in the other order. I read Mörters and Peres Theorem 7.38 on p. 212. The proof has the same steps, but Lévy's characterization replaces Lemma 7.40.
review.why: Accept. All 5 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The proof is the Skorokhod reflection argument of Mörters and Peres. Small doubt: the a.s. limit for all ε ↓ 0 in the hypotheses needs the continuous occupation density. The Tanaka record gives only L² convergence.

step_reviews.why: Tanaka's formula at level 0 with B(0) = 0 gives |B(t)| = W(t) + L(t) for all t, almost surely. The integrand sign(B) is bounded and progressive, so W is a continuous L²-martingale with W(0) = 0.

⟨W⟩_t = ∫₀ᵗ sign(B_s)² ds = t − Leb{s ≤ t : B_s = 0}. Tonelli gives expectation 0 for this measure, because B_s has a density for s > 0. One null set works for all t, because the measure increases with t. Lévy's characterization then shows that W and −W are standard Brownian motions.

The hypothesis gives L(t) − L(s) as a limit of nonnegative terms for rational s < t. If B has no zero on [s, t], the set is empty for small ε. Countably many pairs and the continuity of L give monotonicity and constancy on every interval without zeros.

W̃(s) = L(s) − |B(s)| ≤ L(s) ≤ L(t) for s ≤ t gives M̃(t) ≤ L(t). The last zero s* before t exists because the zero set is closed and contains 0. Step s3 gives L(t) = L(s*) = W̃(s*) ≤ M̃(t). Thus L = M̃ and |B| = M̃ − W̃.
Φ is continuous for uniform convergence on compact sets, so it is Borel. W̃ and B have the same law, the Wiener measure. Thus Φ(W̃) = (|B|, L) has the law of Φ(B) = (M − B, M).

computation_reviews.why: Leb{s ≤ t : |σB_s| ≤ ε} = Leb{s ≤ t : |B_s| ≤ ε/σ}. Division by 2ε gives (1/σ) times (2ε/σ)^(−1) Leb{s ≤ t : |B_s| ≤ ε/σ}. The limit is L(t)/σ.

The identity gives L(t) with the law of M(t). The reflection principle gives M(t) with the law of |B(t)|. Thus E L(t)² = E B(t)² = t and E L^X(t)² = t/σ² = t/(2D). The reflection principle is a standard fact outside the record, which is acceptable in an application.
With t = 100 s and 2D = 1 µm²/s, E L^X(t)² = 100 s²/µm². The root mean square is 10 s/µm. The units of t/σ² are s²/µm², which is correct.
The time in [−ε, ε] is about 2εL^X(t) to first order. Its mean square is (0.02)² · 100 = 0.04 = 1/25 s². The root mean square is 0.2 s. I recomputed both numbers.

step_reviews.why: E[X²] < ∞ gives E|X| < ∞. If a > −∞, then X − a > 0 almost surely, so X − a is not 0 almost surely and E[X − a] > 0. The same argument gives μ < b. At least 1 real value h(x) exists, so m < ∞ and M > −∞.
For x ≠ μ, H(x) = h(x)(x − μ)² by the definition of h, and H(μ) = 0. Thus h(x) ≥ m gives H(x) ≥ m(x − μ)², and the case x = μ is trivial. φ is continuous, so φ(X) is a random variable.

If m < 0, the negative part of H(X) is at most |m|(X − μ)², which is integrable. If m ≥ 0, it is 0. The linear term is integrable with mean 0. Thus E[φ(X)] exists in (−∞, ∞], and E[φ(X)] − φ(μ) = E[H(X)] ≥ m Var(X). Part (ii) is symmetric.

φ′ is differentiable on (a, b), so it is continuous on the closed interval between μ and x. Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder of order 1 gives h(x) = φ″(ξ)/2. Thus inf φ″/2 ≤ h(x) ≤ sup φ″/2 for each x, and this gives (iii). Finite c and C make m and M finite.
For φ(x) = αx² + βx + γ, H(x) = α(x² − μ²) + β(x − μ) − (2αμ + β)(x − μ) = α(x − μ)². Thus h = α and m = M = α. Step s3 then gives equality on both sides.

computation_reviews.why: μ = (5/4 + 7/4)/2 = 3/2. Each value is at distance 1/4 from μ, so Var(X) = 1/16. Both values lie in (1, 2), so the hypotheses of the theorem hold.

φ′(μ) = −1/μ², so the numerator is (μ − x)/(xμ) + (x − μ)/μ² = (x − μ)²/(xμ²). With μ² = 9/4, h(x) = 4/(9x). This function decreases on (1, 2), so m = 2/9 and M = 4/9. h does not attain these values, but they are the infimum and the supremum.
(2/9)(1/16) = 2/144 = 1/72 and (4/9)(1/16) = 4/144 = 1/36. Both m and M are finite, so parts (i) and (ii) apply.
φ″(x)/2 = 1/x³ has its values in (1/8, 1) on (1, 2). The bounds are 1/128 and 1/16, with width 7/128. The window from h has width 1/36 − 1/72 = 1/72, and (7/128)/(1/72) = 63/16.

review.conditions: The last sentence is false as written. It says that E[X] is the unique minimizer for the trivial σ-algebra, with no finiteness condition. review.alignment: I read pp. 1710-1711 of the local copy. Proposition 1 and its proof agree with the excerpt. The source allows atoms on the boundary of S and minimizes over ri(S). The authored version needs X in an open set U. Thus it does not cover KL with atoms at the vertices of the simplex, and the claim that the source statement follows is too strong.
review.why: Defer. All 5 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. The statement and the alignment need 2 changes. First, write: 'For the trivial σ-algebra, E[X] minimizes s ↦ E[d_φ(X, s)] over U. It is the unique minimizer if E[d_φ(X, E[X])] < ∞.' Second, say in the alignment that the record covers the source only when all atoms lie in the open set U.

step_reviews.why: Convexity of g gives g′(0) ≤ 2(g(1/2) − g(0)). Strict convexity gives 2(g(1/2) − g(0)) < g(1) − g(0). Thus d_φ(x, y) = g(1) − g(0) − g′(0) > 0 for x ≠ y. A differentiable convex function has a continuous gradient, so ∇φ is Borel.

I expanded the 3 divergences. All φ terms cancel, and the remainder is ⟨∇φ(z) − ∇φ(y), x − z⟩. The set {Z ∉ U} is in G and has probability 0. Thus the change of Z on this set gives a version of E[X | G] with values in U.

The definition of E[X | G] gives E[1_B (X − Z)] = 0 for B ∈ G, and linearity extends it to simple V. Uniform approximation and the integrable bound sup|V| · |X − Z| extend it to bounded G-measurable V. W is G-measurable, so A_k ∈ G and |1_{A_k} W| ≤ k.

On A_k the cross term is at most k|X − Z| in absolute value, so it is integrable. Its mean is 0 by step s3. The other 2 terms are nonnegative. Thus the expectation of the sum is the sum of the 3 expectations in [0, ∞].

W is finite at each point, so A_k increases to Ω. Monotone convergence for the 3 nonnegative terms gives the identity in [0, ∞]. Uniqueness follows when E[d_φ(X, Z)] < ∞. The last sentence only identifies the constants, so it does not support uniqueness without this finiteness condition.

computation_reviews.why: G = σ(T), and E[X | T] = 3T/2 is the Gamma mean. E[d(X, Z)] is finite for both losses, so the uniqueness part applies. A forecast g(T) that differs from 3T/2 at T = 1 or at T = 2 differs on an event of probability 1/2.
E[X] = E[3T/2] = (3/2 + 3)/2 = 9/4. The constant 9/4 is σ(T)-measurable. E[d(X, Z)] is finite, so the excess E[d(X, 9/4)] − E[d(X, Z)] equals E[d(Z, 9/4)].
(3/2 − 9/4)² = 9/16 and (3 − 9/4)² = 9/16. Their mean is 9/16, so the excess squared error is 9/16.
Z/Y is 2/3 or 4/3. The sum 2/3 + 4/3 − 2 is 0, so the excess is −(log(2/3) + log(4/3))/2 = (1/2) log(9/8). I computed 0.05889, which agrees with ≈ 0.0589.

step_reviews.why: With m = Σᵢ νᵢ xᵢ, the terms φ(xᵢ) cancel, and Σᵢ νᵢ (xᵢ − m) = 0 removes the term with ∇φ(m). The difference is d_φ(m, y), which is nonnegative for convex φ. The chord argument makes it positive for y ≠ m when φ is strictly convex.
By (a), the mean y minimizes the C¹ function z ↦ Σᵢ νᵢ F(xᵢ, z) on the open set U. Fermat's theorem along each coordinate gives Σᵢ νᵢ G(xᵢ) = 0. The point mass at y gives G(y) = 0.

The weights s/(1 + s) and 1/(1 + s) give mean y, so s h(v) + h(−sv) = 0. The case s = 1 gives oddness on B(0, 2ρ), and then h(tv) = t h(v) for small v and tv. The 3-point law and oddness give additivity. Thus L is linear, and the 2-point identity extends L = h to all v with y + v ∈ U.
M(y)(x + εeⱼ − y) − M(y)(x − y) = εM(y)eⱼ. Thus M(y)eⱼ is a difference quotient of 2 maps that are continuous in y by hypothesis. So each column of M is continuous on U.

The fundamental theorem of calculus applies to t ↦ F(x, y_t), which is C¹ near [0, 1]. The insertion of ∇_y F(x, y) = M(y)(x − y) gives A(y) and B(y) as stated. M is bounded on the compact convex hull of y₀ and a small closed ball around y, so dominated convergence gives continuity of A.

F ≥ 0 gives φ(x) ≥ φ(y) + ⟨g(y), x − y⟩, with equality at x = y. Thus φ is a supremum of affine functions. The 2 subgradient inequalities give 0 ≤ φ(y + w) − φ(y) − ⟨g(y), w⟩ ≤ |g(y + w) − g(y)| |w|. Continuity of g makes this o(|w|). A function χ that equals its tangent plane at each point is affine.

A convex function on [0, 1] that meets its chord at an interior point equals the chord. Differentiability then gives d_φ(b, a) = 0 and d_φ(a, m) = d_φ(b, m) = 0. For the 2-point law on {a, b}, both a and m give expected loss 0, which is the minimum. This contradicts uniqueness.

computation_reviews.why: ∂_y[(x − y)²/y] = (−2(x − y)y − (x − y)²)/y² = −(x − y)(x + y)/y². A form M(y)(x − y) needs M(y) = −(x + y)/y² for all x ≠ y, which is impossible. By the reduction in the statement, a law with at most 3 values has a mean that is not optimal.
((1 − 2)² + (3 − 2)²)/2 = 1. Division by y = 2 gives E[F₁(X, 2)] = 1/2.

∂_y F₂ = −x/y² + 1/y = −(x − y)/y², so M(y) = −1/y². For φ = −log x, d_φ(x, y) = x/y − log(x/y) − 1 = F₂. The identity of step s1 gives the excess 2/y − log(2/y) − 1. I checked it numerically at y = 1.5 and y = 2.5.

step_reviews.why: All φ terms cancel in d_φ(x, y) − d_φ(x, z) − d_φ(z, y), and the remainder is ⟨∇φ(z) − ∇φ(y), x − z⟩. With z = x*, the sign of this term decides the Pythagorean inequality. The chord argument with strict convexity gives d_φ(u, v) > 0 for u ≠ v.

The point x_t lies in C ⊆ U, and φ is differentiable at x*. The chain rule gives g′(0+) = ⟨∇φ(x*) − ∇φ(y), x − x*⟩. Minimality makes all difference quotients nonnegative, so g′(0+) ≥ 0. Step s1 turns this into the Pythagorean inequality.
Step s2 with x* = x₁ and x = x₂ gives d_φ(x₂, y) ≥ d_φ(x₂, x₁) + d_φ(x₁, y). The 2 minimal values are equal and finite, so d_φ(x₂, x₁) ≤ 0. Step s1 then gives x₂ = x₁.
The hypothesis and the identity of step s1 give d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x, x*) + d_φ(x*, y). Since d_φ(x, x*) ≥ 0, d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x*, y) for all x ∈ C. Thus x* is a minimizer.

The line through x* and x lies in L. U is open, so x_t ∈ U ∩ L = C for small |t|. Thus g has an interior minimum at t = 0, and Fermat's theorem gives g′(0) = 0. The identity of step s1 then gives equality.

computation_reviews.why: (1 − 1/2)/2 = 1/4. The candidate (1/2, 1/4, 1/4) has positive entries, sum 1 and x₁ = 1/2, so it lies in C. C is convex and y lies in U, so the hypotheses hold.

∇φ(x) = (log x₁, log x₂, log x₃). log(1/3) − log(1/2) = log(2/3), and log(1/3) − log(1/4) = log(4/3). With x₂ + x₃ − 1/2 = 1/2 − x₁, the inner product is −(x₁ − 1/2) log 2 ≤ 0 on C. I checked it at 5 random points of C.
The converse part applies, so x* is the minimizer. (1/2) log(3/2) + 2 · (1/4) log(3/4) = (1/2) log(9/8). I computed 0.058892, which agrees with ≈ 0.0589.
x = (3/4, 1/8, 1/8) lies in C. The gap is −⟨∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*), x − x*⟩ = (x₁ − 1/2) log 2 = (1/4) log 2. A direct computation of the 3 divergences gives 0.17329, which agrees with ≈ 0.173.

step_reviews.why: φ(t) = t log t has its minimum −1/e at t = 1/e, so ∫ φ(f) dP is defined. The density of a mixture is the mixture of the densities. Pointwise convexity of φ then gives convexity of D(·‖P) and finiteness on segments.

Chord slopes of a convex function from a fixed end point do not decrease, so q_{1/k} decreases to the right derivative q₀. The 3 cases of q₀ are correct. Monotone convergence for q₁ − q_{1/k} ≥ 0 gives ∫ q_{1/k} dP → ∫ q₀ dP in [−∞, ∞). The limit is ≥ 0, so q₀ is integrable and P(f* = 0 < f) = 0.

Midpoints lie in E, so D(M‖P) ≥ D*, and step s5 sends D(Q_m‖M) + D(Q_n‖M) to 0. Pinsker's inequality gives the Cauchy property in total variation. computation_reviews.why: (0 · 4 + 1 · 2 + 2 · 1)/7 = 4/7. The constraint E_Q[H] ≤ 4/7 holds with equality, so Q* ∈ E and the constraint is active.

log₂(Q*(k)/P(k)) = log₂(3 · 2^(−k)/Z) = log₂(3/Z) − k. Q* has full support, so the decomposition holds for every Q. log₂(12/7) − 4/7 = 0.20618. The gap 4/7 − E_Q[H] is ≥ 0 on E, so part (b) applies. Bits only rescale all divergences by 1/ln 2.

Under the start from π, the path probability is π(x₀) times the product of the steps. Repeated use of detailed balance moves π to x_n and reverses each factor. The result is the probability of the reversed path, so the 2 laws are equal.

With the support condition, Ψ(x, y) > 0 gives π(y)Ψ(y, x) > 0, so a(x, y) > 0 and P(x, y) > 0. A Ψ-path from x to y ≠ x without its loop steps is a P-path. For x = y, a step to a neighbor and back is a return path. The step omits this trivial case.

computation_reviews.why: π = (4/7, 2/7, 1/7) is the normalization of (1, 1/2, 1/4). a(0, 1) = (1/7)/(4/7) = 1/4 and a(1, 0) = min{1, 4} = 1. a(1, 2) = (1/7)/(1/7) = 1 and a(2, 1) = (1/7)/(1/7) = 1. Only ratios of π occur, so the normalization cancels.

The plain rule gives P(0, 1) = 1/2, P(1, 0) = 1/2, P(1, 2) = (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4 and P(2, 1) = 1. The birth-death ratios are 1 and 1/4, so the law is (4/9, 4/9, 1/9). This is not (4/7, 2/7, 1/7), so the Hastings factor is necessary.

step_reviews.why: Stationarity gives Var A_f(t) = 2∫_0^t (t − s)⟨P_s f, f⟩ ds, as on p. 80. Reversibility gives ⟨P_s f, f⟩ = ‖P_{s/2} f‖² ≥ 0, so t⁻¹ Var A_f(t) increases to σ_f². The spectral theorem gives the Laplace transform ⟨f, (λ − L)⁻¹ f⟩. Monotone convergence and Lemma 9.3.4 give σ_f² = 2‖f‖²_{−1}.

The resolvent u_λ solves λu_λ − Lu_λ = f. The pairing with u_λ and the duality ⟨f, ψ⟩ ≤ ‖f‖_{−1}‖ψ‖_1 give both bounds. The record writes λ‖u_λ‖² with the square, which corrects a misprint on p. 85. The bound ‖Lu_λ‖_{−1} ≤ ‖u_λ‖_1 is also on p. 85.

The bounded family u_λ has a weakly convergent subsequence in H_1. Mazur's lemma and the Cauchy property of −Lv_n give ‖w‖²_1 = ⟨w, f⟩. The liminf chain gives norm convergence, so strong convergence and λ_n‖u_{λ_n}‖² → 0. The uniqueness of w uses λu_λ → 0 weakly in H_{−1}, as on p. 88.

Dynkin's formula for u_λ in the domain of L gives the martingale M_λ. The relation Lu_λ = λu_λ − f gives A_f = M_λ + ζ_λ exactly. The identity E M_λ(t)² = 2t‖u_λ‖²_1 is (9.3.4) of the source. Strong convergence in H_1 makes M_λ(t) Cauchy in L², and E M(1)² = 2‖w‖²_1 = σ_f².

Cauchy-Schwarz gives E(λ∫_0^t u_λ)² ≤ λ²t²‖u_λ‖², and stationarity bounds the 2 end terms by ‖u_λ‖². With λ = 1/t the bound is 9λ‖u_λ‖², which tends to 0 by s3. The martingale part gives 2‖u_{1/t} − w‖²_1 → 0. This is Proposition 9.3.2 of the source.

The remainder t^(−1/2)ζ(t) tends to 0 in L², so also in probability. Proposition 9.1.1 applies to M, which has stationary ergodic increments and E M(1)² = σ_f². Slutsky's theorem then gives t^(−1/2)A_f(t) ⇒ N(0, σ_f²).

computation_reviews.why: Lf(x) = γ(−x − x) = −2γf(x), so P_s f = e^(−2γs)f. Since f² = 1, ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ = e^(−2γs), and σ_f² = 2∫_0^∞ e^(−2γs) ds = 1/γ. The hypotheses hold: μ is uniform, reversible and ergodic, and f is bounded with mean 0.
(λ − L)f = (λ + 2γ)f, so u_λ = f/(λ + 2γ). The limit w = f/(2γ) satisfies −Lw = f. Then 2⟨w, f⟩_μ = 2/(2γ) = 1/γ, which agrees with a1.
Since −Lw = f, M(t) = w(η_t) − w(η_0) + A_f(t) is the Dynkin martingale of w. The remainder w(η_0) − w(η_t) has absolute value at most 2/(2γ) = 1/γ. So t^(−1/2)ζ(t) → 0, and A_f(t)/√t ⇒ N(0, 1/γ).
X(t) = vA_f(t), so X(t)/√t ⇒ N(0, v²/γ). The variance 2Dt gives D = v²/(2γ). With v = 20 μm/s and γ = 1/s, D = 400/2 = 200 μm²/s, and the units are correct.
With a = 2γ, 2∫_0^t (t − s)e^(−as) ds = 2t/a − 2(1 − e^(−at))/a². Times v², this is (v²/γ)(t − (1 − e^(−2γt))/(2γ)). So Var X(t)/t → v²/γ = 400 = 2D, which matches the expected value.

review.why: All 5 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The derivative ∂⟨ω_A⟩/∂K_C is a covariance, so (ii) gives monotonicity in every coordinate. I recomputed Z = 19/2, ⟨σ₁⟩ = 15/19 and the derivative 60/361. A finite difference agrees.

step_reviews.why: Z_K is a finite sum of positive terms. Each exponential is an absolutely convergent series, and the product and the sum over ω are finite. So the expansion and the change of order are valid, as in (3.56) of the source.
The product ω_A∏ω_C^(n_C) equals ∏ω_i^(m_i). The sum over ω factorizes, and each factor is 2 or 0. The coefficients K_C^(n_C)/n_C! are nonnegative, so ⟨ω_A⟩_K ≥ 0 for every nonnegative family K.
For independent copies ω and ω', E[ω_Aω'_B] = ⟨ω_A⟩_K⟨ω_B⟩_K. So E[ω_A(ω_B − ω'_B)] is the covariance of ω_A and ω_B. The multiplication by Z_K² gives the stated double sum.

The map (ω, ω') ↦ (ω, ω'') is a bijection, because ω_i² = 1. Then ω'_C = ω_Cω''_C, and the identities for ω_A(ω_B − ω'_B) and ω_C + ω'_C are correct. The relation ω_Aω_B = ω_{AΔB} completes the change of variables.

For fixed ω'', 1 − ω''_B ∈ {0, 2} and K''_C ∈ {0, 2K_C}. Step s2 applies to K'' ≥ 0, so each inner sum is nonnegative. The derivative of ⟨ω_A⟩_K in K_C is the covariance of ω_A and ω_C, which is nonnegative by (ii).

computation_reviews.why: With the couplings outside Λ at 0, the spins outside Λ are independent of the spins in Λ. So ⟨σ_A⟩ does not change. The increase of these couplings to β keeps all couplings nonnegative, so monotonicity gives ⟨σ_A⟩_Λ ≤ ⟨σ_A⟩_Λ'.
A bounded monotone sequence has a limit. For 2 sequences of boxes that grow to ℤ^d, each box of one sequence is inside a box of the other. So the 2 limits are equal, and the argument is correct.
The weights are e^(J+2h) = 8, e^(J−2h) = 1/2 and e^(−J) = 1/2 for each mixed pair. So Z = 19/2, ⟨σ₁σ₂⟩ = (15/2)/(19/2) = 15/19 and ⟨σ₁⟩ = 15/19. I recomputed all values.
σ₁·σ₁σ₂ = σ₂, so the derivative is ⟨σ₂⟩ − ⟨σ₁⟩⟨σ₁σ₂⟩. This equals 15/19 − 225/361 = 60/361 > 0. A finite difference in J gives 0.16620, which agrees.

nm:statphys-simon-lieb-inequality.why: Source claim: Theorem B.1 on pp. 36-37 of Aizenman, arXiv:2509.02850 v3, states (B.1) with the same graph G_{S,x}. The source says that the inequality has a useful role in rigorous studies of critical phenomena. It also lists analogues for percolation, XY models and random operators. The record has no use evidence, so I judged the scores partly from the mathematics. Inference: the inequality gives exponential decay from a finite-volume criterion, so res is 3 and pra is 2. The proof needs random currents and a switching lemma, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs J_e ≥ 0, zero field, free boundary condition and x ∉ S. The set S must meet every path from x to y. The condition x ∉ S forces x ≠ y. The case y ∈ S is correct, with ⟨σ_yσ_y⟩ = 1. The statement is true as written.
review.prerequisites: nm:union-bound gives the sum over u in step s3. nm:statphys-switching-lemma states the lemma for one graph only. Step s4 proves the graph and subgraph form with the same multigraph bijection, so the step is complete. Lemma 4.2 of the source is this form.
review.alignment: I read pp. 36-38 and Lemma 4.2 on p. 8 of the local copy. Theorem B.1 defines G_{S,x} as in the record, with no edges between sites of S. The record follows the alternative RCR proof on p. 38. The source indicator in (B.5) names x and y, but the sum over u needs x and u, as the record writes.
review.why: All 5 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. Step s4 gives a complete proof of the switching identity for a graph and a subgraph. I recomputed the 4-cycle values with a full sum over 16 spin configurations. The values 8/17, 10/17 and 1/2 agree.

step_reviews.why: The expansion of each factor and the sum over σ give ⟨σ_A⟩_H = ∑_{∂n=A} w_H(n)/Z_H. The zero current gives Z_H ≥ 1. The inserted factor for G_{S,x} equals 1, so the double sum is exact.

In each cluster of edges with n_e > 0 the degree sum is even, so the number of sources is even. Thus x and y lie in one cluster, and a simple path P from x to y exists. The same parity argument applies to a current with sources {x, u}.

P meets S because S separates x from y. Every vertex of P before the first vertex u in S is outside S. So the initial part lies in V_{S,x} and has no edge between 2 sites of S. Thus C_u holds for some u, and the union bound gives the sum.

The identity w_G(n₁)w_{G_{S,x}}(n₂) = w_G(m)∏C(m_e, (n₂)_e) is correct. The sum over n₂ counts subsets K of the multigraph M on the edges of G_{S,x}. On C_u, the symmetric difference with a path K₀ from x to u is a bijection that changes ∂K by B.

With A₁ = {x, y}, A₂ = ∅ and B = {x, u}, the new sources are {u}Δ{y} and {x, u}. The removal of the indicator only increases the sum, because all weights are nonnegative. Step s1 then gives ⟨σ_uσ_y⟩_G⟨σ_xσ_u⟩_{G_{S,x}}, and the sum over u gives the inequality.

computation_reviews.why: From x, the vertices a and b are reached first and are in S. Every path to y goes through a or b first, so y is not in V_{S,x}. G_{S,x} is the tree with edges xa and xb, so each correlation is tanh(βJ) = 1/2.
On the 4-cycle the even edge sets are ∅ and the full cycle, so Z is proportional to 1 + t⁴. The 2 paths of length 2 give 2t² = 1/2. So ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩ = (1/2)/(17/16) = 8/17, and a full sum agrees.
The edge sets with odd degree only at a and y are the edge ay and the path a, x, b, y. So ⟨σ_aσ_y⟩ = (t + t³)/(1 + t⁴) = (5/8)/(17/16) = 10/17. A full sum gives 0.5882, which agrees.
The right side is 2·(1/2)·(10/17) = 10/17, and 8/17 ≤ 10/17 holds. The ratio (10/17)/(8/17) = 5/4 = 1 + t². The values are correct.

review.conditions: The record asks for a finite graph, couplings J_e ≥ 0, β ≥ 0, free boundary, zero field and 4 distinct vertices. The source uses unit couplings. The identity has no division, so it is also true when µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] = 0.
review.prerequisites: Step s2 applies nm:statphys-switching-lemma with F = 1, and the lemma gives exactly what the step uses. The parity count in s3 uses the degree-sum formula without a prerequisite. This fact is elementary.
review.alignment: Exercise 34 on p. 42 of the source states U₄ = −2µ[σ_A]P^{A,∅}[all connected]. The alignment correctly says that the record allows any J_e ≥ 0 and writes the identity without division. Lemma 4.3 is on p. 41.
review.why: All 4 proof steps are correct. I checked the worked example by exact enumeration of the 16 spin states and by a sum over pairs of currents. The values U₄ = −128/289 and P[C₄] = 8/17 are correct.

step_reviews.why: The Taylor series of each factor and the sum over σ give 2^|V| Σ_{∂n=B} w(n), because Σ σ_v^k is 2 for even k and 0 for odd k. This is (4.4)-(4.5) of the source. The product formulas follow directly.
The switching lemma with F = 1 and the pair (B, C) gives the claim. For distinct vertices BΔC = A. For a set C with 2 points, F_C is the event that the 2 points are connected.

Each cluster of the trace of n₁ holds an even number of sources, by the degree-sum formula. The clusters of (n₁ + n₂)^ are unions of these. So exactly 1 of the 4 events occurs, and the indicator sum is 1 + 2·1[C₄].
With s1 to s3, the term with 1 cancels µ[σ_A] and leaves −2Z⁻² Σ w w 1[C₄]. Nonnegative weights give U₄ ≤ 0. Division by Z²µ[σ_A] gives the form of the source.

computation_reviews.why: The even subgraphs of the 4-cycle are the empty set and the full cycle. So the denominator is 1 + t⁴ = 17/16 at t = 1/2. Also tanh((1/2) log 3) = 1/2 is correct.
For neighbours, (1/2 + 1/8)/(17/16) = 10/17. For opposite vertices, 2·(1/4)/(17/16) = 8/17. Exact enumeration of the 16 spin states gives the same values.
Each vertex of the cycle has degree at most 2, so an edge set with 4 odd vertices is a perfect matching. The 2 matchings give 2t² = 1/2, thus 8/17.
8/17 − 2(10/17)² − (8/17)² = (136 − 200 − 64)/289 = −128/289. Exact spin enumeration gives −0.44291, which agrees. The value is below 0, as the theorem states.
(128/289)/(16/17) = 8/17. A direct sum over pairs of currents on the cycle also gives P[C₄] = 0.470588, which is 8/17.

review.conditions: The record asks for β > 0, a symmetric Q with zero diagonal and Q_ij ≥ 0, and µ in [0, ∞)^n. These are the conditions of Lemma 1 and model (1) of the source. Repeated indices are allowed, and the proof covers them.
review.prerequisites: The record lists no prerequisite result. The proof uses only finite sums, an orthogonal change of variables and power series with nonnegative coefficients. No catalog result is necessary.
review.alignment: Lemma 1 on p. 11 of arXiv 2012.05784v1 states the sign of the third derivative. The source gives no proof and cites Lebowitz 1974 in Section 4.6, as the alignment says. The alignment also says that the concavity clause is an added direct consequence.
review.why: All 5 proof steps are correct. I checked the bijection and the rule for S in s3 for all exponents from 0 to 4. I also checked the sign for 300 random systems of 4 spins. The magnetizations 0, 1/2 and 15/19 are correct.

step_reviews.why: log Z_n is the cumulant generating function in µ, so the third derivative is the joint cumulant. I expanded the replica product. Its 8 terms give the 5 cumulant terms with the correct signs.

The matrix with rows (1,1,1,1)/2, (1,1,−1,−1)/2, (1,−1,1,−1)/2 and (1,−1,−1,1)/2 is orthogonal, so it keeps the quadratic form. The identities x¹ − x² = c + d, x¹ − x³ = b + d and x¹ − x⁴ = b + c are correct.
The 16 points split into 8 points with one coordinate ±2 and 8 points that go onto {v : v₁v₂v₃v₄ = −1}. I checked the bijection and the rule for S for all exponents from 0 to 4.

The exponential has nonnegative coefficients because Q ≥ 0 and µ ≥ 0. The 6 listed monomials have mixed parities in (b, c, d) and give 0. For the 2 others the number of all-odd sites is odd, so each product is ≤ 0.
The derivative of log Z_n in µ_i is E[X_i]. Two more derivatives along v give Σ v_j v_k ∂³ log Z_n. Each term is ≤ 0 at µ + tv ≥ 0, so the map is concave on [0, ∞).

computation_reviews.why: With Z = e^J u + e^J/u + 2e^(−J), the formula m = e^{2J}(u² − 1)/(e^{2J}(u² + 1) + 2u) is correct. It gives m = 0 at u = 1 and 12/24 = 1/2 at u = 2.
At u = 4, 4·15/(4·17 + 8) = 60/76 = 15/19. Direct enumeration of the 4 states gives 0.789474, which agrees.
The fields 0, (1/2) log 2 and log 2 are equally spaced, and v = (1, 1) ≥ 0. The gap 1 − 15/19 = 4/19 > 0 agrees with concavity.

review.alignment: Lemma 4.3 on p. 13 and its proof on pp. 13-14 match the outline. But the source sandwich with the constant 9/4 is false for x > √2 − 1. The alignment does not say this, and it must say it.
review.why: Defer. Step s4 states Z(G_nn, x)² ≤ (9/4) max{P^{−1,−1}, P^{−1,1}, P^{1,−1}}, and this is false for x > √2 − 1. On the 3 × 3 torus at x = 0.6, Z² = 369.9 but (9/4) max P = 259.5. The limit in s5 does not change.

step_reviews.why: exp(βσσ) = cosh β (1 + xσσ) on the 2n² edges, and the sum over σ keeps only even subgraphs. This gives the factor (cosh β)^(2n²) 2^(n²). The free energy splits as the step states.

I checked the symbol through Lemma 4.1. Its product over the root grids equals the squares of Proposition 2.1 on the 3 × 3 and 4 × 4 tori at x = 0.6. The bound (x² + 2x − 1)² and the integrability argument are correct.
Lemma 4.1 of the source gives the product formula. The 3 grids with ε = −1 or η = −1 do not contain (1, 1), so every factor is positive by s2.

The lower bound P^{−1,1} ≤ Z² is correct. The upper bound with 9/4 is false for x > √2 − 1. On the 3 × 3 torus at x = 0.6, Z² = 369.9 but (9/4) max P = 259.5. Use Z ≤ A_{1,−1} + A_{−1,1} + A_{−1,−1} = 3Z₀₀ + Z₁₀ + Z₀₁ + Z₁₁, which gives Z² ≤ 9 max P.
The Riemann sums converge to the integral, with the log bound at x = √2 − 1. The limit needs only a sandwich with some fixed constant. So the conclusion stays true after the fix of s4.
1 + x² = cosh(2β)/cosh²β and 2x(1 − x²) = sinh(2β)/cosh⁴β are correct. The factor cosh⁻⁴β gives −2 log cosh β after the integral with 1/(8π²). This cancels the term 2 log cosh β of s1.

computation_reviews.why: cosh²(2β) = 1 + s², and cos θ₁ + cos θ₂ ≤ 2 with equality only at the origin. Because s > 0, the integrand is at least (s − 1)².
For e^(2β) = 3, s = (3 − 1/3)/2 = 4/3 and (4/3 − 1)² = 1/9. A positive lower bound near this β makes the parameter integral analytic.
For s = 1, 1 + 1 − 2 = 0 at θ₁ = θ₂ = 0. The log of the integrand is singular at that point but stays integrable, as s2 shows.
(s − 1)² = 0 only for s = 1, and sinh(2β) = 1 gives e^(2β) = 1 + √2. This is the known βc, which nm:statphys-ising-2d-critical-temperature proves.

Inference: Pirogov–Sinai theory is the standard method for low-temperature phase diagrams without symmetry, so eff 4 and res 4. The method also applies to lattice gases and crystal models, so pra 3 and rea 3. The result needs large β and a small region near the triple point, so hyp 2. The proof needs contours, truncated weights and cluster expansions, so pro 1. The worked example needs the full phase diagram, so app 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs d ≥ 2 and β > β0. It uses U with |λ|, |h| ≤ ρ/8 and ρ = 5^(−d), and the smaller region Ǔ for parts (3)-(5). These are the conditions of the source theorems.
review.prerequisites: The Kotecký–Preiss criterion gives the cluster expansion in steps s3-s5. The implicit function theorem gives h(λ) in s6. The DLR existence result and the short-range-correlation criterion for extremality give the Gibbs measures in s7.
review.alignment: The alignment is honest. It states the join of Theorems 7.36 and 7.41 and the slope bound 4ε/(1 − 2ε) in place of 2ε. It also states the cutoff with |intγ| and the name κ(β). I checked that 4ε/(1 − 2ε) is the correct bound.
review.why: All 7 outline steps state correct claims, and the cited proofs in Sections 7.3 and 7.4 supply them. All 5 application steps are correct. A small point: in s7, Λ in F_(Λᶜ) means a box that contains B(2n). This is not a reason to defer.

step_reviews.why: The claim is correct. Each edge with ω_i ≠ ω_j costs at least 1, and each incorrect site lies in i + B(2) for an endpoint i. This gives ρ = 5^(−d), and ‖W‖ ≤ ρ/4 on U gives ρ0 = ρ/2.
The contour representation with external contours and the ratio Z^#′/Z^# on interiors is (7.29)-(7.31) of the source. The claim is correct, and the cited proof supplies it.
The classes by |intγ| and the C¹ cutoff χ match Definition 7.33. χ = 1 on (−∞, ρ0/4] and χ = 0 on [ρ0/2, ∞). The use of |intγ| is necessary for (7.79), and the alignment states it.
Proposition 7.34 supplies the induction. From (7.79) and (7.80), ŵ ≤ e^(−(½βρ0 − 4)|γ̄|), which is less than e^(−τ|γ̄|) with τ = ½βρ0 − 6. Theorem 7.29 and Lemma 7.31 give (7.85).

Theorem 7.35 supplies this step. The bound (7.85) makes ĝ^#_n a Cauchy sequence, and the Kotecký–Preiss criterion gives a C¹ limit with derivative bounds ε. The identity ψ = max ψ̂^# is the content of Theorem 7.35.
The implicit function theorem for G = ψ̂⁺ − ψ̂⁰ gives h(λ). G_h ≥ 1 − 2ε and |G_h − G_λ| ≤ 4ε give |h′ + 1| ≤ 4ε/(1 − 2ε). The one-sided derivatives of a maximum of C¹ functions give part (4).

Theorem 7.41 and Lemma 7.42 supply this step. The joint law of µ^#_Λ and µ^#_Δ with #-surrounding sets gives (7.100). Extremality follows from short-range correlations, and the Peierls bound gives µ^#(σ_0 = #) ≥ 1 − κ(β).

computation_reviews.why: Correct. At P = (−1/400, 1/1000), e⁺ = −1/1000 + 1/400 = 3/2000 and e⁻ = 1/1000 + 1/400 = 7/2000. Both are positive, so η⁰ is the unique ground state.
Correct. δ = 1/1000 satisfies 2ε < δ < 1/400, and P lies in Ǔ. Part (3) gives h(λ) > 3/2000 > 1/1000 = h, so P is outside the closed sets U⁺_β and U⁻_β.
Correct. At Q = (1/400, 0), e^± = −1/400 < 0. Part (3) gives h(λ) < −1/400 + 1/1000 = −3/2000 < 0, so Q lies in U⁺_β, and by symmetry in U⁻_β.
Correct. G > 0 near Q because G increases in h and h(λ) < 0. The jump of ∂ψ/∂h is at least 2 − 2ε, and ε < 1/2000 gives more than 1999/1000.

nm:statphys-mcbryan-spencer.why: Source claim: Friedli and Velenik, Theorem 9.12 on page 429, give the power-law upper bound for the two-dimensional XY model. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the bound is the rigorous upper half of the spin-wave picture of the BKT transition, so eff 4 and res 3. Its use stays mostly inside models with O(2) symmetry, so pra 2 and rea 2. Part (a) holds for every β > 0, so hyp 3. The proof needs only a complex shift of the angles and a Dirichlet energy bound, so pro 3. The worked bound needs only explicit arithmetic, so app 3.

review.conditions: Part (a) holds for every β > 0 and ‖j − i‖₂ ≥ 3, with R = (‖j − i‖₂ − 1)/2 ≥ 1. Part (b) needs ε ∈ (0, 1) and β ≥ β_0(ε). The statement gives both conditions.
review.prerequisites: Cauchy's integral theorem (wd:Q834025) moves the path of each angle to [−π, π] + i r_j in step s2. Periodicity of the integrand cancels the vertical sides. No other result is necessary.
review.alignment: The alignment is honest. The source bound in (b) has no factor e^(1/β), and the record says so. The record also says that it replaces the Green function by a dipole of logarithmic profiles.
review.why: All 6 proof steps are correct. I checked the cosh bound, the disjoint supports and the Dirichlet energy 2π log R + 4 + 2π. The constant (2 + π)/π² + log 3/(2π) = 0.6958 < 0.7 is correct. All 4 application numbers are correct.

step_reviews.why: The DLR equations write ⟨S_0 · S_k⟩_µ as an average of finite-volume expectations with boundary conditions η. So a bound that is uniform in η and n gives the bound for µ.
The integrand is entire in each angle and 2π-periodic. So Cauchy's theorem on a rectangle moves each path to [−π, π] + i r_j, and the vertical sides cancel. The normalization Z does not change.

The modulus of exp(β cos(x + iy)) is exp(β cosh y cos x). The inequality cosh(tu) − 1 ≤ u²(cosh t − 1) holds for |u| ≤ 1. So the shift costs at most a factor exp(β(cosh t − 1) E), with E the Dirichlet energy of r/t.
g is 1-Lipschitz, g(0) = log R and g = 0 for |x| ≥ R. The supports of h_0 and h_k have no common edge, because a common edge needs ‖k‖ < 2R + 1, which is false.
Jensen gives the edge bound. The line integral ∫x²/(x² + y²)² dx is π/(2|y|). The line y = 0 gives 2(1 − 1/R), and Σ 1/y ≤ 1 + log R. The total S ≤ 2π log R + 4 + 2π is correct.
With t = 1/(2πβ), the exponent of R is −(2 − q)/(2πβ) and the constant is q(4 + 2π)/(4π²β). For (b), (2 + π)/π² + log 3/(2π) = 0.6958 < 0.7, and 3^(1/(2πβ)) ≤ e^(1/β) covers ‖k‖ < 3.

computation_reviews.why: Correct. (2 − 1101/1100)/10 = 1099/11000 = 0.09991. The exponent is also at most 1/10, because q ≥ 1.

nm:statphys-infrared-bound.why: Source claim: Friedli and Velenik, Theorem 10.24 on page 461, state the infrared bound for O(N)-type models on the even torus. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the bound started the reflection-positivity method of Fröhlich, Simon and Spencer, so eff 4 and res 4. It applies to many classical spin models and some quantum models, so pra 3 and rea 3. It needs reflection positivity, a Gaussian nearest-neighbour term and an even torus, so hyp 2. The proof needs Gaussian domination and a second variation, so pro 2. The worked example is a direct substitution, so app 3.

review.conditions: The statement needs L ≥ 4 even, β > 0 and a nonzero finite ρ with compact support. L ≥ 4 is necessary. For L = 2 each vertex has d neighbours, and −Δα = 2ε(p)α fails.
review.prerequisites: The extreme value theorem gives a maximizer of Z in s1. Dominated convergence gives continuity of Z. Fubini gives the Gaussian integral of the crossing edges. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the reflection inequality in s3. Taylor's theorem (wd:Q1137206) gives the second variation in s5.
review.alignment: The alignment is honest. The right side ν/(4βε(p)) equals the source bound. The record states the added condition L ≥ 4 and the Gaussian integral that replaces Lemma 10.28.
review.why: All 7 proof steps are correct. The minimal-N argument works because N(h*⁺) + N(h*⁻) = 2(N − N_c) ≤ 2N − 2. A Gaussian free field check gives equality 1/(4βε(p)) for each component. All 4 application steps are correct.

step_reviews.why: The integrand is at most 1 and ρ is finite, so Z is continuous. Z(h + c) = Z(h), so the maximum over fields with h_0 = 0 on a compact set exists by the extreme value theorem.
For even L ≥ 4, a reflection through edges is a graph automorphism. With γ = N(0, 2βI), each crossing edge factor is an average of a T⁺ factor times a T⁻ factor. Fubini justifies the exchange.
After relabel with Θ, the T⁻ factor is the complex conjugate of a T⁺ factor. Cauchy–Schwarz in the Gaussian variables gives Z(h)² ≤ Z(h⁺)Z(h⁻). The claim is correct.

For the reflection through a disagreement edge, N(h*⁺) + N(h*⁻) = 2(N − N_c) ≤ 2N − 2. So one of h*⁺ and h*⁻ is a maximizer with a smaller N. This contradicts minimality, so the constant field is a maximizer.
φ(λ) = ⟨exp(−2βλX − βλ²Q)⟩ is smooth and has a maximum at λ = 0. The second derivative at 0 gives 2β⟨X²⟩ ≤ Q. The sum of the bounds for Re h and Im h gives the complex case.
For L ≥ 3 each vertex has 2d distinct neighbours, so −Δα = 2ε(p)α. Summation by parts gives X and Q for the plane wave, and s5 gives the bound for ⟨|Σ S^ℓ_i e^{ip·i}|²⟩.
Translation invariance makes ⟨S_i^ℓ S_j^ℓ⟩ a function of j − i. The sum over ℓ and division by |T_L| give ν/(4βε(p)). The second form follows from Σ_{j∼0} cos(p·j) = 2Σ_k cos p_k.

computation_reviews.why: Correct. On the unit sphere ‖S_i − S_j‖² = 2 − 2S_i · S_j, so the weight is the Heisenberg model with constant 2β per edge. The uniform measure on S² has compact support, and L = 4 is even.
Correct. With p = (π/2, π/2, 0), ε(p) = (1 − 0) + (1 − 0) + (1 − 1) = 2. This p is in T*_4 and is not 0.
Correct. ν/(4βε(p)) = 3/(4 × 1 × 2) = 3/8 for ν = 3 and β = 1.
Correct. At β = 0 only j = 0 contributes, and ⟨S_0 · S_0⟩ = 1. So the ratio is 3/8. The absolute value 64 × 3/8 = 24 for ⟨|Ŝ_p|²⟩ is also correct.

nm:statphys-fss-continuous-symmetry-brea.why: Source claim: Friedli and Velenik, Theorem 10.25 on page 462, and Peled and Spinka, Theorem 2.13, state the result. It gives long-range order for O(N) models in d ≥ 3 at large β. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: this was the first proof of long-range order with a continuous symmetry, so eff 4 and res 4. The method applies to many reflection-positive models, so pra 3 and rea 3. It needs reflection positivity, d ≥ 3 and large β, so hyp 2. The proof rests on the infrared bound, so pro 2. The worked example needs a finite sum and the Watson integral, so app 3.

review.conditions: The statement needs d ≥ 3, unit spins, an even torus with L ≥ 4 and β > 0. d ≥ 3 makes β₀ finite. L ≥ 4 is the condition of the infrared bound.
review.prerequisites: The infrared bound gives s2. Dominated convergence with the bound 9dπ²/(8|q|²) gives s5. The record nm:parseval-s-identity is the circle form, but s1 uses the finite DFT form. The finite form is elementary, so this is a small gap.
review.alignment: The alignment is honest. I checked that the source constant equals β₀, because 1 − (1/2d)Σcos(p·j) = ε(p)/d. The record states the added uniform bound from Peled and Spinka, Theorem 2.13.
review.why: All 5 proof steps are correct. The cubes C_p have volume (2π)^d/|T_L|, and 1 − cos t ≥ 2t²/π² holds for |t| ≤ π. All 4 application numbers are correct. The application uses s1-s2 for the finite-volume bound, and it says so.

step_reviews.why: The vectors |T_L|^(−1/2) e^{ip·j} form an orthonormal basis, and ‖S_j‖ = 1. So Σ_p ‖Ŝ_p‖² = |T_L|², and the p = 0 term is |T_L|² ‖m_L‖². The finite DFT form is elementary.
The unit sphere is compact, so the infrared bound applies with L ≥ 4 even. Translation invariance gives ⟨‖Ŝ_p‖²⟩ = |T_L| Σ_j e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0 · S_j⟩. The expectation of s1 then gives the bound with R_L.
With representatives in {−L/2 + 1, …, L/2}^d, the cubes C_p are disjoint and have volume (2π)^d/|T_L|. So R_L is the integral of a step function f_L over a subset of [−π, π]^d.
1 − cos t ≥ 2t²/π² for |t| ≤ π is correct. For q ∈ C_p with p ≠ 0, |q|_∞ ≤ 1.5|p|_∞, so f_L(q) ≤ 9dπ²/(8|q|²). This bound is integrable for d ≥ 3 and gives K_d.
For each q ≠ 0, the centre p_L(q) tends to q, so f_L(q) → 1/ε(q). Dominated convergence with the bound of s4 gives R_L → 4β₀/ν. Then the liminf bound 1 − β₀/β follows.

computation_reviews.why: Correct. For L = 4, 1 − cos p_k takes the values 0, 1, 2, 1. So each coordinate has the generating function (1 + x)², and 3 coordinates give (1 + x)⁶.
Correct. ε(p) = 3 − Σ cos p_k, so W is the Watson integral 0.50546. Then β₀ = (3/4)W = 0.3791, and 1 − 0.3791 = 0.621 at β = 1.

nm:statphys-chessboard-estimate.why: Source claim: Peled and Spinka, Proposition 2.16 on page 30, state the chessboard estimate for reflection-positive models on the torus. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the estimate is a standard tool for proofs of phase transitions and long-range order, so eff 4 and res 3. It applies to spin models, lattice gases and dimer models, so pra 3 and rea 3. It needs reflection positivity, so hyp 2. The proof uses only Cauchy–Schwarz and an extremal assignment, so pro 3. The worked example needs a 2 × 2 transfer matrix, so app 3.

review.conditions: The statement needs h ≥ 0 symmetric and bounded, Z > 0, and reflection positivity for the reflection R. It is correct as written. The worked example must check reflection positivity, because the theorem needs it.
review.prerequisites: Cauchy–Schwarz (nl:16121) for the positive semidefinite form E[F(σ)G(Rσ)] gives s2 and s3. Other reflections come from torus symmetries. No other prerequisite is necessary.
review.alignment: The alignment is honest. The record writes out the density, the form (40), the assumption Z > 0 and the sign change. These match Proposition 2.16 of Peled and Spinka.
review.why: All 5 proof steps are correct. Step a4 claims P(σ_0 = −1) ≤ 1/3 for every value of J. This is false for J < 0, because reflection positivity fails. Restrict the claim to J ≥ 0.

step_reviews.why: R is an automorphism and h is symmetric, so Rσ has the same law as σ. This gives the symmetry of the form. Reflection positivity gives positive semidefiniteness, and Cauchy–Schwarz applies.
With F and G as defined, (F, G) = P(τ), (F, F) = P(τ⁰) and (G, G) = P(τ¹). So s1 gives P(τ)² ≤ P(τ⁰)P(τ¹). Other reflections through edges come from torus symmetries.
For a maximizer τ* with least N, a reflection through a disagreement edge gives N(τ⁰) + N(τ¹) = 2N − 2N_c < 2N. Both reflected assignments are maximizers, so one has a smaller N. Thus τ* is constant.
With g_v = f_v/(a_v + δ)^(1/|Λ|), each new a_w is less than 1, so s3 gives a ratio at most 1. The limit δ → 0 gives the bound with Π a_v^(1/|Λ|).
|Λ| = (2L)^d is even, so a_{v_0} does not change when f_{v_0} changes sign. Then s4 applies to both signs and gives the bound for |E Π f_v(σ_v)|.

computation_reviews.why: Correct. h(a, b) = 5/4 + (3/4)ab gives 2 and 1/2. The crossing edges of R are {0, 1} and {−1, 2}. Their expansion gives nonnegative weights times squares, so reflection positivity holds.
Correct. With f_0 = 1_{−1} and f_v = 1 otherwise, a_0 = P(σ ≡ −1) and a_w = 1 for w ≠ 0. So the estimate gives P(σ_0 = −1)⁴ ≤ P(σ ≡ −1).

(128/11753)^(1/4) = 0.3230 is correct. But the claim P(σ_0 = −1) ≤ 1/3 for every value of J is false. For J < 0, h = cosh J + (sinh J)ab has a negative weight, so reflection positivity fails. At J = −0.5 the exact value is 0.402, and as J → −∞ it tends to 1/2. Correction: claim the bound 1/3 only for J ≥ 0.

nm:statphys-wilson-algorithm.why: Source claim: Lyons and Peres state the result as Theorem 4.1 on p. 99 and prove it with Lemma 4.2 on pp. 100-101. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the method is the standard exact sampler for weighted spanning trees and links random walks to electrical networks, so res is 4. The cycle-popping proof needs a careful coupling of the stacks, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite irreducible chain and a root r. The tree law is proportional to Ψ, the product of p(x, y) over edges oriented toward r. For a connected network the law is proportional to Ξ. These conditions match Theorem 4.1 of the source.
review.prerequisites: The only listed prerequisite is wd:Q25378690, the Ionescu-Tulcea theorem. It gives the independent stack entries in s1. A product measure gives the same family. The loop erasure and the cycle pops are defined in the record, so no catalog result is absent.
review.alignment: I read pp. 99-101 of the local copy of Lyons and Peres. Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 agree with the excerpt. The alignment field says correctly that the record generalizes Lemma 4.2 to the present top edge at each vertex.
review.why: All 7 proof steps are valid and follow the cycle-popping proof of the source. Step s6 does not state one easy inclusion, and the source is equally short. I recomputed all 4 application steps on the triangle with conductances 1, 2 and 3. Each value is correct.

step_reviews.why: The stack entries S_i^x are independent with law p(x, ·). The Ionescu-Tulcea theorem gives a valid probability space for this countable family. The colors and the top edges are well defined.
The claim generalizes Lemma 4.2 of the source to the present top edge at each vertex, not color 1. The case analysis for a cycle C′ that shares a vertex with C_k is correct.
Step s2 applies after each pop. Thus every procedure pops exactly the set 𝒞 of poppable cycles and stops with the same tree T. This matches the conclusion on p. 101 of the source.
Wilson's method reads the top entries and pops each erased loop as a visible cycle. The last-visit argument for the loop erasure is short but correct. So the method is one procedure of step s3.
Each history fixes finitely many entries, and the next move reads a new entry. So each move has law p(u, ·) given the past. The (1 − ε)^k bound shows that each walk stops almost surely.

The product formula P((𝒞, T) = (O, t)) = Ψ(t) times the cycle weights is correct. The step does not state that {(𝒞, T) = (O, t)} is inside the cylinder event. This inclusion is easy, and the source is equally short.
For a network p(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x), so Ψ(t) = Ξ(t) π(r)/∏ π(x). The last factor does not depend on t. Each spanning tree has exactly 1 orientation toward r, so the law is proportional to Ξ.

computation_reviews.why: From 1 the walk goes to 0 with probability 1/3. A return from 2 to 1 erases the loop. So a = 1/3 + (2/3)(2/5)a, and I recomputed a = 5/11.
Given the path ⟨1, 0⟩, the walk from 2 hits 0 with probability 3/5. So the tree {01, 02} has probability (5/11)(3/5) = 3/11. I recomputed this value.
The tree {01, 12} has probability (5/11)(2/5) = 2/11, and {12, 02} has 6/11. The weights Ξ are 3, 2 and 6 with sum 11. So the law is proportional to Ξ.
P(01 ∈ T) = 3/11 + 2/11 = 5/11. The parallel sum of 1 and 5/6 is (5/6)/(11/6) = 5/11. With c(01) = 1 this agrees with the Kirchhoff formula.

nm:statphys-varopoulos-carne.why: Source claim: Lyons and Peres state the bound as Theorem 13.4 on p. 432 and prove it on pp. 433-434. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the bound gives a Gaussian upper bound on every reversible graph, and random walk theory and group theory use it often. The proof needs spectral theory and Chebyshev polynomials, so pro is 2. Conf is medium because the prerequisite wd:Q7820874 has an open identity conflict.

review.conditions: The statement needs a reversible random walk on a countable connected graph with conductances c and π(x) = Σ_y c(x, y). The bound holds for all x, y and n ≥ 1 with d = d(x, y). These conditions match Theorem 13.4 of the source.
review.prerequisites: Cauchy-Schwarz, Tonelli, the binomial theorem, de Moivre, diagonalization, Markov and monotone convergence each support the step that cites them. The prerequisite wd:Q7820874 has an open identity conflict, because the Wikidata item is a different Tonelli theorem. The use in s1 is correct.
review.alignment: I read pp. 432-434 of the local copy of Lyons and Peres. Theorem 13.4 and Lemma 13.5 agree with the excerpt. The source gets (13.11) with Hoeffding-Azuma, but the record uses a Chernoff bound. The alignment field does not say this.
review.why: All 7 proof steps are valid. The truncation to finite B and the monotone limit are correct additions to the source proof. Steps a1, a2 and a3 are correct. Step a4 has a loose sentence about the √n scale, but its main claim of order √(n log n) is correct.

step_reviews.why: P is self-adjoint because c(x, y) is symmetric. Cauchy-Schwarz and Tonelli give ‖Pf‖_π ≤ ‖f‖_π. The step states the symmetry before it shows absolute convergence. This order is minor, because later steps use only finite B.
P_B is self-adjoint on H_B with ‖P_B‖ ≤ ‖P‖_π. The path sum gives p_n^B(x, y) = √(π(y)/π(x)) (f_x, P_B^n f_y)_π. A path from x to y has at least d steps, so (f_x, P_B^i f_y)_π = 0 for i < d.
The binomial theorem and de Moivre's formula give s^n = Σ_k q_n(k) T_k(s) for s = cos θ. Both sides are polynomials in s, so the identity holds for the operator S. This matches the source proof.
S is self-adjoint on the finite space H_B with ‖S‖ ≤ 1. In an orthonormal eigenbasis T_k(S) has the entries T_k(λ_j), and |T_k(λ_j)| ≤ 1. So ‖T_k(S)‖ ≤ 1.
T_k(S) is a polynomial of degree |k| in S, so the terms with |k| < d are 0 by step s2. Cauchy-Schwarz and step s4 bound each other term by 1. The bound with Σ_{|k|≥d} q_n(k) follows.

Markov's inequality gives P(S_n ≥ d) ≤ e^(−λd)(cosh λ)^n. The term bound gives cosh λ ≤ e^(λ²/2), and λ = d/n gives e^(−d²/(2n)). Symmetry gives the factor 2. The source uses Hoeffding-Azuma, but this argument is also valid.
The bound from steps s5 and s6 does not depend on B. For finite B_m that increase to V, the path sums increase to p_n(x, y) by monotone convergence. So the bound holds for p_n(x, y).

computation_reviews.why: With 4 ≤ π ≤ 8 on ℤ² with conductances in [1, 2], the ratio π(y)/π(x) is at most 8/4 = 2. So the prefactor is at most 2√2. Step s1 gives ‖P‖_π ≤ 1.
40²/(2 · 100) = 1600/200 = 8. I recomputed 2√2 e^(−8) = 9.49 × 10^(−4). This agrees with the record value of about 9.5 × 10^(−4).
ℤ² has 4j sites at ℓ¹ distance j, and p_n = 0 beyond distance n. I recomputed 8√2 Σ_{j=60}^{100} j e^(−j²/200) = 2.29 × 10^(−5). This agrees with the record.
The claim of order √(n log n) is correct. But the a3 bound is about 8√2 n e^(−r²/(2n)), which grows with n for r = c√n. So write: the bound is small once r ≥ √(2(1 + δ) n log n).

nm:statphys-gaussian-correlation-inequal.why: Source claim: Latała and Matlak give the proof of Royen as Theorem 2 and Section 2 of arXiv 1512.08776. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the inequality solved an old conjecture and gives simultaneous confidence regions, so hyp is 4. The proof needs Laplace transforms, Schur complements and gamma-type densities, so pro is 1 and level is research.

review.conditions: The statement needs a centered Gaussian measure on ℝ^d and closed convex symmetric sets K and L. Theorem 1 of the source omits the word convex, but the abstract and the proof need it. The record states convexity correctly.
review.prerequisites: Hahn-Banach, dominated convergence, the principal axis theorem, Weinstein-Aronszajn, the determinant expansion, Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus each support the step that cites them. Step s5 uses uniqueness of the Laplace transform, which is not listed. The source also only states it.
review.alignment: I read Theorem 2, Section 2 and Lemmas 4-8 in the local copy of arXiv 1512.08776. The outline names the real ingredients in the correct order. The source writes h_τ(t_J, ·) where it means s_J, and the record correctly writes s_J.
review.why: All 6 outline steps have correct claims, and the cited proof supplies each of them. I recomputed all 4 application steps. The set K is a closed convex symmetric sublevel set, so the theorem applies. The joint bound 361/400 and the Bonferroni value 9/10 are correct.

step_reviews.why: Hahn-Banach separation writes a closed symmetric convex set as a countable intersection of symmetric strips. The limits for t_i = 0 and for C + εI are correct because the boundary events are null. This gives Theorem 2 of the source.

C(τ) is a convex combination of 2 positive definite matrices, so it is positive definite. At τ = 0 the blocks are independent, so F(1) ≥ F(0) is the claim. Lemma 6 of the source gives the derivative under the integral.

For |z| ≥ r + 1 the points z + τh with τ ≥ 1 − 1/‖h‖ lie in B(0, r + 1). The integral of (1 − τ) over that interval is 1/(2‖h‖²), so D ≥ m/4 and F_δ(z) = 0 for δ < m/(4M₀). For |z| < r + 1, D ≥ mη²/2 holds both for η ≤ ‖h‖ ≤ 1 and for ‖h‖ > 1.

Accept. Lemma 1 of Freericks on p. 13 proves this connectivity of the configuration lattice. Each link of the chain is a hop along a bond with t_xy ≠ 0, so each matrix element in the product is nonzero.

Accept. Π⊥ on both sides removes the K terms, and positivity gives W^(1/2)L_xΠ⊥ = 0. Products of L_x and 1 − L_x give every Π_X, so step s4 makes the range of W the whole space. A singular real combination W₁ + λW₂ then gives a contradiction.

Accept. The S^z_tot = 0 sector has finite dimension, and its lowest eigenvalue is simple for every U > 0. So the Riesz projection P(U) is continuous. Tr(P(U)S_tot·S_tot) is continuous with values in a discrete set, so it is constant on (0, ∞).
